youtube_title: Kingsford Heights, Indiana: the wartime town where most houses stood empty
youtube:
You asked for Kingsford Heights! In 1942, the government built a whole town in LaPorte County for workers at the Kingsbury Ordnance Plant. It was first called Victory City. Thousands of homes went up, on streets laid out in long curves instead of a grid. But many workers kept their own homes and commuted to the plant, and most of the new houses stood empty. A 1944 newspaper headline called it a "New Deal Ghost Town." Hundreds of the houses were packed up and shipped off to cities like Evansville and Green Bay. The families who stayed bought the land from the government and incorporated the town, and today empty lots still dot its curving streets. Comment your town, and it could be next! #KingsfordHeights #LaPorteCounty #Indiana #WW2 #History #LaPorteAfterDark #Shorts

All pictures are drawn. Narration is a computer voice. Sources: Town of Kingsford Heights (townofkingsfordheights.com); Jeff Kenney, "Victory City," Towne Post (2022); The History Museum, South Bend; "New Deal Ghost Town," Garfield County News (Panguitch, Utah), Sept. 28, 1944, via Utah Digital Newspapers; Indiana Public Media, A Moment of Indiana History (Indiana Magazine of History); Clio, "Diamond Villa Housing" (Evansville); Wisconsin Historical Society, property record HI245038 (Green Bay); Indiana Division of Historic Preservation and Archaeology survey, via Wikipedia. More LaPorte County history: https://laporteweathernow.com/history

factcheck: Blind independent check Nov. 16, 2026 (script, on-screen text and pictures only), then a second check of the changes: 'Nearly 3,000 houses went up' became 'Thousands of homes went up' (3,000 planned; 2,974 in the 1944 story; 'more than 2,600 dormitories, trailers, and prefabricated homes' per IMH); the headline card names the Garfield County News, Sept. 28, 1944 (Utah Digital Newspapers record), without '(UTAH)', which isn't printed on the scan; 'bought the town' became 'bought the land from the government and incorporated the town'; the unverifiable aerial ring plan was dropped and 'curved in rings around a town center' became 'laid out in long curves, not a grid'; first label '1940s'. Second check: all supported.
